The zero moment makes the mass of any feasible density equal to its integral against the affine hinge input. Pointwise comparison against the positive part bounds the mass by the hinge integral. The accepted Hausdorff estimate holds at every real base. Centering at the moving marks preserves convergence. If the limiting centered body contains rB, its support function is at least r, so a Hausdorff error delta gives the two homothetic bounds at ratios 1−delta/r and 1+delta/r. Inclusion by zero extension and the Lebesgue change of variables give the two bounds on T and continuity at interior limiting marks.

At an own-boundary limit, for fixed R the test hinge gives an upper bound by the same moment inequality, even if the approximating marks are boundary marks. Hausdorff convergence of full-dimensional bodies gives convergence of their indicators off the null boundary, and on one bounded region the hinges converge boundedly for fixed R. In the limiting body the hinge tends to zero away from its null supporting plane and is bounded by one. Sending R to infinity gives the zero boundary limit.

Interior approximations in each fixed input fiber and continuity on the whole hull extend the concavity inequality, including zero boundary values, zero weights, and base rank zero. The mass has degree d under a simultaneous homothety of the body and mark, so its root has degree one.
